November 2, 2026 Key Takeaways Trusted AI starts with visibility. Businesses need to understand where AI is operating, what it can access and how it is being used. Protection belongs in the architecture. As AI agents take on more tasks, endpoint security and isolation can help organizations establish boundaries and contain risk. Confidence enables adoption. Clear governance, supported by HP and its channel partners, can help customers move from experimentation to responsible AI use. AI is increasingly moving from the cloud to where work happens every day: on the device. Alongside opportunities for performance and user experience, local AI processing can help organizations keep sensitive data and corporate intellectual property within their environment. Realizing those benefits requires visibility, protection and governance at the endpoint. In an interview with CRN , James Wright, Global Head of Personal Systems Security Solutions at HP, explains why AI security must start at the endpoint, the importance of visibility and isolation, and the opportunity for channel partners to guide customers through the next phase of enterprise AI. Visibility is the starting point “Problem number one is visibility,” Wright says. Organizations need to understand which AI tools are operating across their environment, what they can access, and where unsanctioned use may be emerging. Without that understanding, it becomes harder to establish meaningful boundaries or make informed decisions about adoption. For businesses, visibility should be part of the adoption process. Decisions about access, oversight and accountability should develop alongside decisions about where AI can deliver value. Build protection into the foundation Agentic AI introduces new risks as autonomous agents gain access to data, interact with systems and take action across workflows. It also gives attackers greater automation and speed, potentially making previously lower-risk areas more attractive targets. Organizations need to understand and govern what agents can access and do, while building security into their AI architecture from the outset. Wright points to isolation as one existing endpoint capability with relevance to these emerging challenges. "HP already uses isolation technology across a number of our security products to contain potentially malicious activity within secure environments. The same underlying approach can be relevant to some of the security challenges emerging around agentic AI because it can help reduce the available attack surface," Wright explains. HP’s work across both hardware and software allows the company to consider security throughout the endpoint architecture. As Wright explains, that gives HP additional options for designing protection into the device from the outset. Turn confidence into adoption Channel partners have an important role in connecting these priorities to each customer’s environment. Their knowledge of customers’ infrastructure and business needs can help translate uncertainty into concrete decisions about protection and deployment. For HP, helping businesses adopt AI means helping them establish the conditions for responsible use. Security needs a place in those conversations from the beginning. As Wright puts it: “We need greater governance and control to give businesses the confidence to embrace it.” Read the full interview here .
